title: Preventing Violence Against Children (Global Commitments)
summary_md:
Governments are stepping up action to protect children from violence, with over 230 new pledges to be announced at the Second Global Ministerial Conference on Ending Violence Against Children in Manila, Philippines taking place on 18-19 November, the World Health Organization (WHO) said today.

New pledges include Tanzania’s planned US$ 190 million investment in child protection; Nepal’s pledge to halve school violence by 2030, benefiting 4.2 million children; Chile’s commitment to protect more than 3.4 million children from school violence and cyberbullying; and Mexico’s commitment to strengthen online protection by 2030. Burundi has also pledged to ban corporal punishment by 2028, while Côte d’Ivoire aims to reduce violence against children by 30% by 2030.

The commitments, including first-time pledges from 30 countries, bring the global total to more than 630 pledges from 140 countries, since the first conference held in Bogotá, Colombia, in 2024. The commitments mark a significant step up in global efforts to address violence against children, which affects more than 1 billion children worldwide each year.

“Violence against children is preventable and not inevitable," said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General. "And yet, many children continue to suffer harm that can affect their health and well-being throughout their lives. WHO commends the governments making commitments to end violence against children and calls on them to fulfil those commitments by investing in proven solutions that protect children before violence occurs, while ensuring those who experience violence receive the care and support, they need.”

Every day, children experience physical, sexual or psychological violence, often in places where they should feel safe; homes, schools and communities. An estimated 400 million children under five regularly experience physical punishment and/or psychological violence at the hands of parents and caregivers. One in five women and one in seven men report having experienced sexual abuse during childhood.

Violence against children can have lifelong, damaging consequences for health and can cause immediate physical, mental and emotional harm, while also increasing the risks of chronic disease, disability and high-risk behaviours later in life. Repeated exposure to violence can compound these effects.

Evidence shows that childhood violence is associated with a 66% higher risk of depression in adulthood, twice the likelihood of adolescent pregnancy, a 34% higher risk of HIV infection and increased risks of alcohol use disorders, heart disease and diabetes. An estimated 141 000 suicides each year are attributable to childhood sexual abuse.

Co-organized by the Government of the Philippines, WHO and UNICEF, the conference will bring together representatives from 130 governments and more than 1300 participants, including children, young people, survivors and civil society, to accelerate prevention, investment and accountability. The meeting will focus on scaling up proven approaches, including supporting parents and caregivers, making schools safer, and strengthening health and child protection services. It will also address emerging threats, including violence facilitated by digital technologies and heightened risks during humanitarian emergencies and climate-related crises.

WHO is calling on countries to increase sustained investment in prevention, strengthen accountability and ensure that children experiencing violence receive timely, appropriate support. Health systems have a critical role in identifying abuse, providing safe, child-centred care and connecting children with protection services.

title: Institute of Philanthropy and WHO launch partnership to advance healthy ageing in the Western Pacific
summary_md:
The Institute of Philanthropy and the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for the Western Pacific are deepening their partnership on healthy ageing. At its centre is a new four-year healthy ageing initiative involving WHO and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) to advance approaches that enable older people to maintain functional ability and live well in their communities. Supported by the Institute and The Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust through a contribution of approximately US$ 7 million, the initiative forms part of a wider programme of work tied to the UN Decade of Healthy Ageing (2021–2030).

The initiative comprises two complementary components:
- In Hong Kong SAR (China), CUHK, working with WHO and supported by the Charities Trust, will develop and test a Multi-component Healthy Ageing Package.
- A regional component supported by the Institute will develop adaptable guidance and tools, work with interested Member States on country adaptation and demonstration and strengthen regional learning and evidence generation.

Starting in 2027, the collaboration will generate evidence, develop regional guidance on healthy ageing, support countries to adapt it to their own contexts, and strengthen regional learning. Participants at the high-level technical meeting shared experience and practical lessons on prevention, primary health care, community-based and integrated care, the health and care workforce, and stronger links between health and social support.

Population ageing is accelerating across the Region. More than 245 million people in the Western Pacific are aged 65 or older, and that number is projected to double by 2050. But healthy life expectancy has not kept pace: the gap between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy widened from 9.1 years in 2000 to 10.0 years in 2023.

WHO’s Regional Action Plan on Healthy Ageing in the Western Pacific provides a framework for helping older people maintain functional ability and live well in their communities. It emphasizes prevention and health promotion, primary health care, integrated health and social care, community-based support and enabling environments.
content: The Institute of Philanthropy and the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for the Western Pacific are deepening their partnership on healthy ageing. At its centre is a new four-year healthy ageing initiative involving WHO and The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) to advance approaches that enable older people to maintain functional ability and live well in their communities. Supported by the Institute and The Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust through a contribution of approximately US$ 7 million, the initiative forms part of a wider programme of work tied to the UN Decade of Healthy Ageing (2021–2030). The initiative comprises two complementary components. In Hong Kong SAR (China), CUHK, working with WHO and supported by the Charities Trust, will develop and test a Multi-component Healthy Ageing Package. Building on this experience, a regional component supported by the Institute will develop adaptable guidance and tools, work with interested Member States on country adaptation and demonstration and strengthen regional learning and evidence generation. Starting in 2027, the collaboration will generate evidence, develop regional guidance on healthy ageing, support countries to adapt it to their own contexts, and strengthen regional learning. The wide-ranging collaboration was introduced at a high-level technical meeting on healthy ageing, co-convened by the Institute and WHO in Manila alongside the seventy-seventh session of the WHO Regional Committee for the Western Pacific. The event brought together delegations from Australia, China, Cook Islands, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia, the Philippines and Singapore, alongside representatives from the Institute, the Charities Trust, CUHK, the World Organization of Family Doctors and the International Federation of Medical Students' Associations. Participants shared experience and practical lessons on prevention, primary health care, community-based and integrated care, the health and care workforce, and stronger links between health and social support. Across diverse country contexts, discussions highlighted the importance of maintaining functional ability and enabling older people to live well in their communities. “The second half of the Decade of Healthy Ageing must be about turning commitments into results,” said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. “This collaboration offers an opportunity to turn evidence into action, adapt solutions to country needs, and learn from what works.” Dr Saia Ma’u Piukala, WHO Regional Director for the Western Pacific, contrasted two 75-year-olds: one whose world has shrunk to “the journey between the couch and the clinic”, the other still out walking with friends. “The gap between them isn't luck,” he said. “It’s built over decades, by the choices we make as individuals and the choices we make as societies.” Population ageing is accelerating across the Region. More than 245 million people in the Western Pacific are aged 65 or older, and that number is projected to double by 2050. But healthy life expectancy has not kept pace: the gap between life expectancy and healthy life expectancy widened from 9.1 years in 2000 to 10.0 years in 2023. WHO’s Regional Action Plan on Healthy Ageing in the Western Pacific provides a framework for helping older people maintain functional ability and live well in their communities. It emphasizes prevention and health promotion, primary health care, integrated health and social care, community-based support and enabling environments. Since the endorsement of the Regional Action Plan in 2020, WHO has worked with Member States across the Region to translate these priorities into national policies, integrated care approaches and age-friendly communities, while generating and sharing practical lessons across different country contexts. The Age-Friendly Cities and Communities initiative now has more than 170 members across nine countries and areas, including all 18 districts in Hong Kong SAR (China). For more than three decades, The Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust has supported age-friendly initiatives across Hong Kong SAR, including support for age-friendly communities. Its long-standing collaboration with CUHK has included community-based programmes that promote older people’s intrinsic capacity and functional ability and strengthen integrated health and social care. Reflecting on the discussion, Dr Gabriel Leung, Director of the Institute of Philanthropy, highlighted many commonalities across countries despite their diverse contexts. “Partnerships and sharing are really what all of this is about,” “There is so much to learn from each other.” The new initiative will build on the experiences and lessons shared through this week’s meeting, strengthening regional learning, technical exchange and evidence generation to inform the adaptation of effective approaches across different country contexts. About the Institute of Philanthropy: The Institute of Philanthropy was established in September 2023 through a strategic seed grant of 6.8 billion Hong Kong dollars (US$ 870 million) from The Hong Kong Jockey Club and its Charities Trust. Established as an independent “think-fund-do” tank for China, Asia and beyond, the Institute is dedicated to promoting philanthropic thought leadership and enhancing sector capabilities at local, regional and global levels in collaboration with fellow funders. It seeks to provide an Asia-based platform bringing global stakeholders together to promote the betterment of societies everywhere. About the work on healthy ageing at WHO in the Western Pacific: The Regional Action Plan on Healthy Ageing in the Western Pacific provides a framework for helping older people maintain functional ability and live well in their communities, with a focus on health system transformation and technological and social innovation. Progress over the past year is set out in the Report of the Regional Director: The work of WHO in the Western Pacific Region, 1 July 2025 – 30 June 2026 (WPR/RC77/2).

title: WHO Western Pacific Member States agree to urgently accelerate progress on key health priorities
summary_md:
Health leaders from across the World Health Organization (WHO) Western Pacific Region concluded their annual meeting after endorsing action plans to address lagging progress on hypertension, tobacco control and immunization, and adopting guidelines for the safe and effective use of artificial intelligence in health care.

Key priority areas endorsed by Member States:
- **Artificial Intelligence in Health:** Endorsed *Guidance for Responsible AI in Health in the Western Pacific Region* that countries can use in designing and rolling out AI safely and effectively in health systems according to specific country needs and capacities.
- **Hypertension Control:** Hypertension impacts one in three adults in the Region and is a silent killer, often masked until severe complications arise, including cardiovascular disease, stroke, disability and premature death. Member States endorsed the *Regional Plan for Accelerating Hypertension Control in the Western Pacific*, calling for integrating hypertension prevention and control as core functions of people-centred primary health care.
- **Immunization Progress:** At a time when measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases are making a comeback, Member States endorsed the *Regional Plan to Accelerate Immunization Progress in the Western Pacific* to strengthen national immunization systems and ensure equitable access to immunization for all.
- **Tobacco Control:** Tobacco causes an estimated 3 million deaths annually in the Region. Member States endorsed *Accelerating Progress towards the 2030 Tobacco Control Target in the Western Pacific Region* to combat tobacco industry interference and aggressive marketing of new products, including e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches, to young people.
content: Health leaders from across the World Health Organization (WHO) Western Pacific Region concluded their annual meeting here today after endorsing action plans to address lagging progress on hypertension, tobacco control and immunization, and adopting guidelines for the safe and effective use of artificial intelligence in health care. Health ministers and more than 200 other participants – representing 2.2 billion people, over a quarter of the world population– gathered for the seventy-seventh session of the WHO Regional Committee for the Western Pacific to address those four urgent issues and other pressing public health concerns. Tackling artificial intelligence, or AI, WHO Member States acknowledged that its significant potential to transform and strengthen health systems also carries risks. After careful consideration, the Regional Committee - WHO’s governing body in the Western Pacific - endorsed an action plan, Guidance for Responsible AI in Health in the Western Pacific Region , that countries can use in designing and rolling out AI safely and effectively in health systems according to specific country needs and capacities. Hypertension, which impacts one in three adults in the Region, is a silent killer, its symptoms often masked until severe complications arise, including cardiovascular disease, stroke, disability and premature death. But detection, treatment and blood pressure control remain unacceptably low in many parts of the Western Pacific. The Regional Committee endorsed the Regional Plan for Accelerating Hypertension Control in the Western Pacific , which calls for integrating hypertension prevention and control as core functions of people-centred primary health care, with particular attention to equity and underserved populations. At a time when measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases are making a comeback, the Western Pacific Region is off track to achieve its immunization targets, particularly among children and underserved populations. Member States endorsed the Regional Plan to Accelerate Immunization Progress in the Western Pacific , which calls for countries to strengthen national immunization systems and services, with a view to identifying and addressing barriers to vaccination and ensuring equitable access to immunization for all - a particular challenge at a time of constrained national budgets and declining donor support. Turning to the final priority on the agenda, Member States endorsed Accelerating Progress towards the 2030 Tobacco Control Target in the Western Pacific Region , a plan to combat one of the leading public health challenges in the Region, which causes an estimated 3 million deaths annually. The acceleration plan addresses recent challenges including tobacco industry interference in policy-making and aggressive campaigns to market new products, including e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches, to young people. Most countries in the Region are not on track to achieve the regional target of a 30% relative reduction in the prevalence of tobacco use by 2030. “While all these steps outlined across the four priority areas build on existing WHO frameworks, our Member States have recognized the urgency in addressing significant gaps and challenges undermining health and well-being,” said Dr Saia Ma’u Piukala, WHO Regional Director for the Western Pacific. “Not only have countries pledged to swiftly tackle these issues, but they have also committed to genuine collaboration regionwide, sharing experiences and lessons learnt through the convening power of WHO, a role we take very seriously,” he added. Besides the four main agenda items, Member States also participated in a ministerial roundtable on exploring voluntary regional collaboration mechanisms to improve access to safe, effective, quality-assured and affordable health products. On the sidelines of the Regional Committee, the Institute of Philanthropy and the Regional Office for the Western Pacific announced a new four-year healthy ageing initiative involving WHO and The Chinese University of Hong Kong to advance approaches that enable older people to maintain functional ability and live well in their communities. Supported by the Institute and The Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust through a contribution of approximately US$ 7 million, the initiative forms part of a wider programme of work tied to the UN Decade of Healthy Ageing (2021–2030) “Over the past four days at the seventy-seventh Regional Committee, Member States have consistently underscored WHO’s role in supporting governments and other health partners, recognition for which we are truly grateful,” said Dr Piukala. “This reiterates WHO’s value-add to countries in our Region and indeed globally, in advancing multilateralism in health – so crucial to our vision and mandate of Health for All.” - END - For more information and/or to arrange media interviews, contact wprocom@who.int For all relevant documents, recordings and other material related to the seventy-seventh session of the WHO Regional Committee for the Western Pacific, visit: https://www.who.int/westernpacific/about/governance/regional-committee/session-77 Health leaders from across the World Health Organization (WHO) Western Pacific Region concluded their annual meeting here today after endorsing action plans to address lagging progress on hypertension, tobacco control and immunization, and adopting guidelines for the safe and effective use of artificial intelligence in health care. title: Mongolia strengthens multisectoral action to accelerate clean household energy transition
summary_md:
ULAANBAATAR, 3 November 2026 – Mongolia brought together high-level government leaders and key stakeholders to advance coordinated efforts towards a clean household energy transition. The National Forum on a Stepwise Approach to Phasing Out Household Coal Use was jointly led by the Ministries of Health; Environment and Climate Change; Urban Development, Construction and Housing; and Energy, and the Governor’s Office of the Capital City, with support from WHO.

At the Forum, the ministries, together with WHO, UNDP and UNICEF, launched the *Call for Action for Clean Energy for Health*, advancing the proposed *Roadmap for a Stepwise Approach to Phasing Out Household Coal Use, 2027–2040*.

**Health Impacts and Current Situation in Mongolia:**
- Household coal use remains a major source of air pollution, particularly in the ger areas of Ulaanbaatar, provincial centres and rural soum centres.
- In 2021, the combined effects of ambient and household air pollution were associated with an estimated 2,895 deaths in Mongolia. Children, pregnant women, older people, and people living with chronic conditions face particularly serious health risks.
- Access to cleaner household energy remains unequal: an estimated 76% of urban residents use clean fuels and technologies for cooking, compared with only 22% of rural residents.

**Targets and Practical Measures:**
- The Government aims to reduce air pollution by approximately 30% in 2025–2026 and completely phase out solid fuel use in Ulaanbaatar by 2040.
- Measures include establishing smoke-free zones in major urban centres, reducing raw coal use, expanding electric and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) heating, improving housing insulation, and ger-area redevelopment.
- To date, 5,000 households in areas with high levels of air pollution have transitioned to LPG heating, 408 households have been connected to solar energy, and 31 coal-fired boiler facilities have been converted to gas and electric heating.
content: ULAANBAATAR, 3 November 2026 – Mongolia brought together high-level government leaders and key stakeholders to advance coordinated efforts towards a clean household energy transition. The National Forum on a Stepwise Approach to Phasing Out Household Coal Use was jointly led by the Ministries of Health; Environment and Climate Change; Urban Development, Construction and Housing; and Energy, and the Governor’s Office of the Capital City, with support from the World Health Organization (WHO). At the Forum, the ministries, together with WHO, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), launched the Call for Action for Clean Energy for Health , mobilizing coordinated action to accelerate Mongolia’s transition to clean household energy and advance the proposed “ Roadmap for a Stepwise Approach to Phasing Out Household Coal Use, 2027–2040 .” The roadmap provides a shared, phased framework for coordinating multisectoral action, guiding investment, and aligning implementation with the country’s health, air quality, energy, climate, housing, and social development priorities. Household coal use remains a major source of air pollution, particularly in the ger areas of Ulaanbaatar, provincial centres and rural soum centres. In 2021, the combined effects of ambient and household air pollution were associated with an estimated 2,895 deaths in Mongolia. Children, pregnant women, older people, and people living with chronic conditions face particularly serious health risks. Access to cleaner household energy also remains unequal. An estimated 76% of urban residents use clean fuels and technologies for cooking, compared with only 22% of rural residents. The transition must therefore respond to the diverse needs of urban, peri-urban, and rural households while ensuring that vulnerable and energy-poor families are not left behind. During the Forum, Minister of Health Batshugar Enkhbayar said: “Transitioning to clean household energy is essential to protecting public health, preventing disease, and creating healthier and safer living environments. Building on existing policies and measures, including restrictions on raw coal use, the introduction of electric and gas heating solutions, and improvements in housing insulation, will be important to accelerating this transition. Mongolia is building on important progress, including the 2019 ban on raw coal use by households in Ulaanbaatar, the expansion of electric and liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) heating, improvements in housing insulation and ger-area redevelopment. Other initiatives include the 100,000 Solar Ger Programme, the 3x100 Clean Energy Initiative and Mongolia's NDC 3.0 commitment. The Government aims to reduce air pollution by approximately 30% in 2025–2026 and completely phase out solid fuel use in Ulaanbaatar by 2040. Its measures include establishing smoke-free zones in major urban centres, reducing raw coal use, and transitioning to gas and other clean energy sources. These efforts are being implemented in phases, including the transition of households, businesses, and public facilities, particularly schools and kindergartens, to electric and gas heating solutions, alongside the reorganization of heating boiler facilities. Minister of Environment and Climate Change Sandag-Ochir Tsend said: “Reducing air pollution requires more than changing fuels or reducing the number of chimneys. It calls for a comprehensive, multisectoral approach that integrates air pollution reduction into urban planning, energy, infrastructure, transport, and building insulation policies.” Together, these efforts provide a strong foundation for an integrated transition that combines clean household energy, energy-efficient housing, enabling infrastructure, sustainable financing, and appropriate social protection. Ulaanbaatar is also advancing practical measures to reduce household emissions and expand access to cleaner energy in ger areas. Governor of the Capital City and Mayor of Ulaanbaatar Purevdagva Byaruuzana highlighted several initiatives being implemented in partnership with development partners. These include a planned 2.4 MW solar power plant with battery energy storage, to be established in partnership with UNDP to support clean energy supply in ger areas. To date, 5,000 households in areas with high levels of air pollution have transitioned to LPG heating, while 408 households have been connected to solar energy. In addition, thirty-one coal-fired boiler facilities have been converted to gas and electric heating. Under the city's “New Ulaanbaatar” policy, further measures are targeting major sources of air pollution, including emissions from household heating and cooking, coal-fired heat-only boilers, and motor vehicles. In introducing the Call for Action , Governor of the Capital City and Mayor of Ulaanbaatar Purevdagva said: “We must accelerate practical solutions that give households access to cleaner and more reliable energy while reducing the sources of air pollution in our city.” The Forum's Call for Action and the proposed Roadmap provide a shared national direction for a healthier future, emphasizing evidence-informed action, integrated and locally appropriate solutions, affordability, and a just transition. Dr Socorro Escalante, WHO Representative to Mongolia, said: “Mongolia’s transition to clean household energy is a public health imperative that calls for action now. Air pollution represents a prolonged, and devastating emergency. It demands an urgent, sustained, and accelerated response.”

title: Mongolia interrupts outbreak-associated measles transmission
summary_md:
Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, 17 November 2026 – The Ministry of Health of Mongolia and the World Health Organization (WHO) announced that transmission associated with the recent measles outbreak has been interrupted.

According to national surveillance data, the last confirmed measles case was reported on 24 August 2026, and no new measles cases have been detected since then. However, surveillance will continue, and this does not imply that the risk of measles has been eliminated completely, as imported cases remain possible.

**Key Public Health Guidance & Takeaways:**
- **Vaccination:** Timely receipt of both recommended measles-containing vaccine doses protects individuals and communities, prevents severe illness and deaths, and stops outbreaks and transmission.
- **Closing Immunity Gaps:** Despite strong progress, some populations, including children, remain unvaccinated or under-vaccinated and therefore at risk.
- **Action for Parents and Caregivers:** Parents and caregivers are encouraged to check their children’s vaccination status with their local health centre and arrange any missed doses promptly.
content: Joint Statement by the Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization (WHO) Country Office in Mongolia Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, 17 November 2026 - The Ministry of Health of Mongolia and the World Health Organization (WHO) announced that transmission associated with the recent measles outbreak has been interrupted. This is an important public health milestone, achieved through strong national leadership, intensified vaccination, sustained surveillance and strong national and local coordination of the outbreak response. According to national surveillance data, the last confirmed measles case was reported on 24 August 2026, and no new measles cases have been detected since then. This sustained absence of outbreak-associated cases suggests that transmission linked to the recent outbreak may have been interrupted. This assessment is based on available epidemiological and laboratory information, but surveillance will continue and the situation will be reviewed if new evidence emerges. This refers specifically to transmission associated with the recent outbreak and does not imply that the risk of measles has been eliminated. Vaccination was central to bringing this outbreak under control. Through intensified routine immunization services, and catch-up and supplementary immunization activities, health workers reached people who had missed vaccination and helped close urgent immunity gaps. These efforts demonstrate a clear and important message: measles vaccines work. Timely receipt of both recommended vaccine doses protects individuals and communities, prevents severe illness and deaths, and stops outbreaks and transmission. This achievement reflects the collective efforts of the Government, the Ministry of Health, the National Center for Communicable Diseases, local health authorities, health-care workers, communities, including parents, caregivers and schoolteachers, and partners. The response also strengthened national and subnational capacities to prepare for and respond to public health emergencies through intensified vaccination efforts, enhanced epidemiological and laboratory surveillance, the rapid investigation of suspected cases, and timely clinical management and care of patients. WHO supported the Government throughout the response by providing technical assistance and strategic guidance on outbreak response coordination, vaccination strategies, surveillance, risk assessment, case management, infection prevention and control, and risk communication. Intensified vaccination activities led by the Ministry of Health have substantially reduced the number of people susceptible to measles. Despite this progress, gaps in vaccination coverage remain, with some populations, including children, still unvaccinated or under-vaccinated and therefore at risk. Continued efforts are essential to reach these populations, close remaining immunity gaps and protect Mongolia from renewed transmission. As measles continues to circulate internationally, imported cases remain possible and could trigger renewed transmission in communities where vaccination coverage is insufficient. “The Government will continue to prioritize the prevention of measles and other vaccine-preventable diseases. Healthcare workers play a vital role in helping parents and caregivers understand the importance of vaccination, answering their questions and providing accurate information. Protecting the progress we have made and preventing future outbreaks is a shared responsibility. Let us work together to protect every child.” — Minister of Health Batshugar Enkhbayar. The Ministry of Health and WHO therefore call for sustained action to ensure that every eligible child receives both recommended doses of measles-containing vaccine on time. Health authorities must continue to use local vaccination coverage, surveillance and risk-assessment data to identify and close immunity gaps in every district and province. Parents and caregivers are encouraged to check their children’s vaccination status with their local health centre and arrange any missed doses. “ The interruption of measles transmission is an important public health achievement. Vaccination remains our most powerful protection against measles, supported by the rapid deployment of response measures, timely public health action, and close coordination between hospitals and public health services. Sustaining this progress means building stronger immunization and public health systems, supporting our health workers, and empowering families and communities to be active partners in safeguarding health. We commend the Government for its leadership and investments, which were crucial in controlling this outbreak while ensuring that the country is stronger and better prepared to protect its people from future public health emer gencies.” — Dr Socorro Escalante, WHO Representative to Mongolia. The Ministry of Health and WHO reaffirm their commitment to sustaining these gains by strengthening routine immunization, reaching all missed and under-vaccinated people, maintaining sensitive epidemiological and laboratory surveillance, and strengthening preparedness to prevent, rapidly detect and respond to future measles outbreaks and other vaccine-preventable disease threats.

title: Mongolia conducts evaluation for HPV vaccines roll-out
summary_md:
Mongolia introduced HPV vaccination in 2024 as part of its cancer elimination programme. By the first quarter of 2026, more than 177,000 children aged 11–14 years have received HPV vaccination.

The Ministry of Health, with support from WHO, conducted a Post-Introduction Evaluation (PIE) to assess implementation progress, identify challenges and generate recommendations:
- **Schedule & Policy:** Adoption of a simple one-dose schedule for both girls and boys, supported by strong collaboration between the health and education sectors.
- **Catch-Up Vaccination:** Targeted follow-up efforts and community outreach successfully increased uptake in areas that initially reported low coverage.
- **Challenges Identified:** Misinformation and anti-vaccine narratives on social media, limited engagement of some private schools, and weak microplanning in certain areas.
- **Recommendations:** Sustain investment in demand generation, social listening, misinformation management, and parent engagement, while positioning schools as a platform for life-course immunization throughout childhood and adolescence.
content: Mongolia introduced HPV vaccination in 2024 as part of its cancer elimination programme. By the first quarter of 2026, more than 177 000 children aged 11–14 years have received HPV vaccination. To assess the success and performance of the vaccination roll-out, the Ministry of Health, with support from the World Health Organization (WHO), conducted a Post-Introduction Evaluation (PIE) to assess implementation progress, identify challenges and generate recommendations for a successful roll-out. The evaluation included assessments at national and subnational levels on programme planning, service delivery, vaccination coverage, communication, community engagement and sustainability. The evaluation has affirmed the progress that has been made, underpinned by a strong policy framework, experience and lessons learned from the HPV introduction in 2012, and the adoption of a simple one-dose schedule for both girls and boys. The evaluation also highlighted the critical role of the strong collaboration between the health and education sectors as a key factor in achieving higher HPV vaccination coverage. In areas where engagement of local governments, schools, teachers and parents were strong, better results were achieved. One good practice is the establishment of joint health–education directives to support high vaccination targets, helping drive significant improvements in coverage. The evaluation emphasized the effectiveness of catch-up vaccination activities. Several locations that initially reported low uptake achieved substantial gains over time through targeted follow-up efforts, demonstrating that early setbacks can be successfully addressed through sustained engagement, flexible service delivery approaches and continued community outreach. At the same time, the PIE identified several implementation challenges. Misinformation and anti-vaccine narratives spread rapidly through social media and communities during the early stages of vaccine introduction, while demand-generation activities and risk communication efforts were not fully established before rollout. Limited engagement of some schools, particularly private schools, weak microplanning, and insufficient coordination between education and health stakeholders also affected implementation. As a way forward, several strategies were identified, including collaboration between the health and education sectors, strengthened accountability and teacher engagement, and greater involvement of local leadership. It is also recommended to sustain investment in demand generation, social listening, misinformation management and parent engagement, recognizing that vaccine confidence must be continuously nurtured rather than addressed through one-time campaigns. The evaluation highlights an opportunity to position schools as a platform for life-course immunization by linking HPV vaccination with other vaccination contacts throughout childhood and adolescence. The lessons learned from HPV vaccine introduction will not only support higher HPV vaccine uptake but also strengthen preparedness for future vaccine introductions and broader adolescent health programmes in Mongolia.

title: Strengthening Mental Health Resilience in the Face of Climate Shocks Across the Western Pacific
summary_md:
As climate change intensifies globally, severe storms, floods, droughts, extreme temperatures and other climate-related hazards are affecting lives, livelihoods and communities across the WHO Western Pacific Region. Beyond physical destruction, these hazards have a significant impact on mental health and well-being.

**Key Facts & Recommendations:**
- Individuals face distress, anxiety, grief, uncertainty and disruptions to social support systems following emergencies, displacement or loss of livelihoods.
- Vulnerable groups—including women, children and adolescents, older persons, persons with disabilities, and communities repeatedly exposed to disasters—face heightened risks.
- The Western Pacific Region is home to more than 200 million people living with mental health conditions.
- WHO convened the Technical Consultation to Promote Mental Health Amid Climate Change and Disasters in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia (15–17 September 2026), bringing together experts from Malaysia, Mongolia, Palau, the Philippines and Vanuatu.
- Countries are working to integrate mental health and psychosocial support into climate adaptation, disaster risk reduction, and emergency preparedness strategies, while strengthening workforce capacity and community resilience.
content: As climate change intensifies globally, its effects are becoming increasingly visible. Across the World Health Organization (WHO) Western Pacific Region, severe storms, floods, droughts, extreme temperatures and other climate-related hazards are affecting lives, livelihoods and communities. Beyond the physical destruction and economic losses lies another important but often overlooked consequence: the impact on mental health and well-being. Across the Region, communities are experiencing the psychological and social consequences of climate change and disasters. Individuals face distress, anxiety, grief, uncertainty and disruptions to social support systems following emergencies, displacement or loss of livelihoods. These impacts can be particularly significant for people already facing vulnerabilities, including women, children and adolescents, older persons, persons with disabilities, and communities repeatedly exposed to disasters. The Western Pacific Region is home to more than 200 million people living with mental health conditions, and many countries continue to face challenges in ensuring equitable access to quality-assured mental health services and support. As climate-related risks increase, countries and areas in the Region are recognizing the need to strengthen mental health and psychosocial support as part of broader efforts to prepare for, respond to and recover from disasters and environmental change. While awareness of the links between climate change and mental health is growing, responses often remain fragmented. Mental health considerations are not always fully integrated into climate adaptation, disaster risk reduction and emergency preparedness strategies. At the same time, countries have identified the need for stronger evidence, practical tools, cross-sectoral collaboration and opportunities to learn from one another’s experiences. To address these challenges, WHO is supporting efforts to strengthen mental health systems and make them more climate-resilient across the Region through the initiative, “ Advancing Mental Health through Innovative and Inclusive Solutions Amid Climate Change and Disasters in the Western Pacific Region” Supported by The Nippon Foundation, this three-year initiative aims to promote innovative and inclusive approaches, strengthen country capacities and generate practical knowledge to support action at national and regional levels. – Dr Huong Thi Giang Tran, Director of Health Promotion, Disease Prevention and Control, WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific To further support country action, WHO convened the Technical Consultation to Promote Mental Health Amid Climate Change and Disasters in the Western Pacific Region in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, from 15 to 17 September 2026. The consultation brought together government representatives, experts and partners from Malaysia, Mongolia, Palau, the Philippines and Vanuatu – a range of countries representing diverse parts of the vast Western Pacific Region – to exchange experiences, discuss emerging evidence and identify practical actions to strengthen climate-resilient mental health systems. – Dr Erdenebayar Namjil, State Secretary of the Ministry of Health of Mongolia Participants reflected on the growing mental health impacts of climate change and disasters, shared country experiences, and explored opportunities for integrating mental health into climate adaptation, disaster preparedness and emergency response efforts. Discussions highlighted the importance of strengthening workforce capacity, generating context-specific evidence and fostering collaboration across sectors. – Dr Socorro Escalante, WHO Representative in Mongolia As the climate crisis increasingly shapes the health landscape of the Western Pacific, countries are working to adapt to evolving environmental challenges, ensuring that mental health is an essential pillar to be incorporated into preparedness, response and recovery efforts. The consultation reflected a shared commitment among countries and partners to better understand and address the mental health impacts of climate change and disasters. By fostering collaboration, strengthening capacities and promoting evidence-based action, countries across the Region are taking important steps towards building more resilient communities and healthier futures. As climate risks continue to evolve, so too must efforts to protect and promote mental well-being. Investing in mental health today will help ensure that communities are better prepared, supported and empowered to face the challenges of tomorrow.
